fullText:
Banger paper from Microsoft Research.

(bookmark it)

They run 1K+ coding agents at once to test a scalable self-organized multi-agent harness.

This is an interesting test because most multi-agent systems today have some hierarchy or structure.

Agensh has no central orchestrator.

It coordinates parallel coding agents through a shared state instead of a central orchestrator.

Each agent gathers context, claims a sub-task, does the work, shares what it found, verifies the result, and merges it, all asynchronously through a shared workspace and a message channel.

On the five hardest ProgramBench tasks with GPT-5.6-sol, increasing agents from 1 to 128 raises the mean final test-pass rate from 19.31% to 28.78%.

Larger teams also reach a given pass rate sooner.

On pandoc, 1,024 agents take the test-pass rate from 33.89% to 55.06%.

The authors also report forms of cooperation that the agents start on their own and that become standard practice as the team grows.

fullText:
4 TYPES OF SWITCHING COSTS FOR DURABLE MOATS

I like switching costs as competitive advantages.

They’re not as powerful as network effects.

But they are way more available. 

Especially to b2b businesses. 

Here are 4 types. I believe this list is originally from Hamilton Helmer (not sure).

1. Financial switching costs.

These are direct monetary losses and contractual penalties incurred during a vendor migration.

Think early cancellation fees, sunk infrastructure spending, and unamortized equipment purchases.  

2. Procedural switching costs

These are operational barriers from necessary retraining and systems integration.

Reorganizing staff routines and reformatting legacy databases can create painful productivity declines.

Which makes switching unappealing.  

3. Relational and risk based switching costs

People avoid switching from a proven vendor because of the risk of unexpected  problems and operational downtime.

Take-aways for managers?

-Don’t rely strictly on financial contracts.

Build softer procedural friction into the operational habits of your customers.

2. Identify the perceived operational risks of a system failure

Position your offering as the most reliable choice in the market.

I hope this framework helps.

An interesting idea is to continually train specialized models on skills.

This paper explores that idea.

They propose SkillGym which turns human-written skills into 2,756 training environments with code-based checkers, then fine-tunes on 8,364 successful trajectories.

That is above the reported scores for Claude Sonnet 4.6 and GPT-5.4 Mini.

With no skills loaded, the trained model beats the base model that has the skills in context.

fullText:
Cool paper on catching alignment failures with Jev.

The ideas is to ask Jev one generic yes/no question about a model's response, and use its probability as a score.

With no extra training, that score separates failures from good responses well, with a median AUROC of 0.886.

It is also cheap. On 19 benchmarks, a Jev pass cost $0.30, while the LLM judges those benchmarks use cost $18.96.

Researchers built RLCDAlignBench from 44 existing benchmarks across ten failure types, including sycophancy, jailbreaks, deception, prompt injection and reward hacking. Jev, TypeSafe AI's calibrated decision model, answers many typed questions about one input in a single call, each with a probability.

On StrongREJECT, it agrees with human labels as well as the GPT-4o-mini scorer does, and ranks responses better (AUROC 0.971 vs 0.929). Where Jev confidently disagreed with benchmark labels, it found label errors in three benchmarks.

They find that the question wording matters little. The thresholds do not transfer between benchmarks, and fitting one on 10 labelled items raises median F1 from 0.706 to 0.793.

Paper: https://t.co/vUZV4k786o
